Lindisfarne
LIN-dis-farn
n. (the tidal island off the Northumbrian coast, also called Holy Island, where Aidan settled in 635 and Cuthbert was bishop)
Old English Lindisfarena ee, the island of the travellers from Lindsey; later called Holy Island from its monastery.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lindisfarne is a tidal island off the Northumbrian coast, cut off by the sea twice a day, and for a century and a half it was the chief church of the north of England. Oswald asked Iona for a bishop and received Aidan in 635; Aidan set his see on the island and went on foot through Bernicia preaching, with the king as his interpreter at first. Finan and Colman followed him, and after the Synod of Whitby had settled the Easter question against the Celtic reckoning, Cuthbert was made bishop in 685 and died on Farne two years later. The Lindisfarne Gospels were written and illuminated in that house about 700, and Eadfrith who made them was its bishop. In 793 the Danes landed, killed and plundered, and Alcuin wrote from the Frankish court in horror; in 875 the community left altogether, carrying Cuthbert's coffin, and after long wandering settled at Durham. The dictionary records Lindisfarne for the pattern of its work, which was a bishop who walked, and for the warning in its end: the house that converted a kingdom was itself burned, and the gospel it carried outlived the buildings that carried it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a bishop as an overseer of a diocese; a flock as a company under one shepherd; to feed as to supply with nourishment; a temple as a place dedicated to divine worship; and waste as desolate, ruined, destroyed.

expand to see more

BISHOP, n. An overseer; a spiritual superintendent, ruler or director; in the primitive church, an elder or overseer of a particular church.

FLOCK, n. A company or collection of sheep or other small animals; a Christian church or congregation, in reference to the pastoral relation.

FEED, v.t. To give food to; to supply with nourishment; to furnish with any thing of which there is continual consumption or waste.

TEMPLE, n. A public edifice erected in honor of some deity, and set apart for divine worship.

WASTE, a. Destroyed; ruined; desolate; stripped of inhabitants; lying unoccupied and untilled.

Key Scripture

Act 20:28 — "Take heed therefore unto yourselves, and to all the flock, over the which the Holy Ghost hath made you overseers, to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood."

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Psa 79:1 — "A Psalm of Asaph. O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled; they have laid Jerusalem on heaps."

Isa 64:11 — "Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire: and all our pleasant things are laid waste."

Modern Corruption

Tidal island off Northumberland where Aidan set his see in 635, Cuthbert was bishop, and the Lindisfarne Gospels were made; sacked by the Danes in 793.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bishop who feeds rather than the bishop who presides. Paul addressed the Ephesian elders as overseers with a flock to tend, “to feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood” (Act 20:28), and Peter put the same charge in a sentence that describes Aidan's practice exactly: “Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2).

The second thing to name is the live temptation to measure the church by its buildings and its books. Lindisfarne had the finest manuscript in Europe and a bishop every Northumbrian knew, and in 793 the heathen came into it and left it a ruin, which is a thing the Psalter already knew how to say: “O God, the heathen are come into thine inheritance; thy holy temple have they defiled” (Psa 79:1). Isaiah grieved over the same loss in the same words we would use for the burnt church on the island, “Our holy and our beautiful house, where our fathers praised thee, is burned up with fire” (Isa 64:11). The men went to Durham and the preaching went on, which is the answer to the grief.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek episkopos (G1985), an overseer; Greek poimaino (G4165), to tend a flock; Hebrew nachalah (H5159), an inheritance; Hebrew saraph (H8313), to burn.

expand to see more

Greek poimaino (G4165) — to tend, to shepherd; “to feed the church of God”, Acts 20:28.

Greek episkopeo (G1983) — to oversee, to exercise the office of overseer; “taking the oversight thereof”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Greek poimnion (G4168) — a flock; “Feed the flock of God which is among you”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Hebrew nachalah (H5159) — an inheritance, a possession; “the heathen are come into thine inheritance”, Psalm 79:1.

Hebrew sherephah (H8316) — a burning; “is burned up with fire”, Isaiah 64:11.

Usage

"“to feed the church of God” (Act 20:28) — what Aidan went on foot to do."

"“not by constraint, but willingly” (1Pe 5:2) — the manner of the Celtic bishops."

"“the heathen are come into thine inheritance” (Psa 79:1) — 793, in the Psalter's words."
